results.summary: This design displays names on a 7-segment display, showing one letter per second by default. The top three input bits select which name is shown, while the lower five bits configure the clock divider speed, allowing a manual push-button to step the display. The bottom eight bits of the internal counter are output on the bidirectional pins. It is based on the 7-segment counter template project and is intended for simple visual demonstrations.

This design implements three different ring oscillators with varying temperature dependence: a basic NAND-based oscillator, a capacitively loaded NAND oscillator, and a tri-state inverter oscillator with sub-threshold enable. Each oscillator drives a counter that can be latched and transferred via a Manchester-encoded serial data stream, and divided versions of each oscillator clock are also output. The design is intended for characterization and testing of oscillator behavior. Silicon tests confirmed that at least one oscillator output works, though full testing is incomplete.

This project is a single leaky integrate-and-fire (LIF) neuron with post-synaptic spike-timing-dependent plasticity (STDP) learning. The documentation is essentially absent, with placeholder text for both the operation and testing sections. The pin names suggest a 7-segment display output and a counter, but the actual functionality cannot be determined from the provided information. No external hardware requirements or notable features are described.

This design implements a configurable leaky integrate-and-fire (LIF) neuron that mimics biological neuron behavior. It uses a state machine to configure parameters such as beta (decay rate) and threshold, then integrates an input current to produce a membrane potential and spike output. The neuron is controlled via input pins for configuration and current injection, with outputs for membrane potential and spike. It is intended for experimentation with neuron parameters and behavior.

This design is a 4-bit wide memory that can operate as either a FIFO or LIFO, selected by a mode pin. It can store up to 30 entries, with full, empty, output valid, and overflow flags. A 7-segment display shows the number of stored entries up to nine, and disables with an overflow flag if more than nine entries are stored. The design is tested by loading and reading data, and it preserves stored data when switching modes.

This design implements a Hodgkin-Huxley neuron model in silicon, which produces action potentials in response to input current injection. An 8-bit input current is applied, interpreted as a 16-bit fixed-point value in uA/cm^2, and the membrane potential is output on both dedicated and bidirectional pins. The neuron fires periodically when the current exceeds a threshold of approximately 12 (in the 8-bit representation). It is intended for exploring neuron dynamics and spiking behavior.

This project contains two compute units that perform ALU operations based on input instructions, with the final output being the XOR of their outputs. The design is controlled by reset and enable signals, and it was tested on EDA Playground with a testbench. The only output pins are for a 7-segment display, suggesting the result is shown visually. The documentation is brief and does not specify the exact ALU operations or instruction format.

This design implements a simple leaky integrate-and-fire (LIF) neuron that integrates an input current and produces a spike when the membrane potential exceeds a threshold. It has inputs for clock, current, and reset, and outputs the next membrane potential and a spike signal. The documentation notes that a current input of 100 after 20 cycles should produce a spike. The design is minimal and intended for basic testing of neuron behavior.

This project claims to implement the Hodgkin-Huxley neuron model, but the documentation describes a clock divider and binary-to-decimal counter for a 7-segment display, with no mention of neuron behavior. The inputs set a compare value to control counting speed, and the bottom 8 bits of the counter are output on bidirectional pins. The documentation appears to be copied from a template and does not match the title. It is likely that the actual neuron implementation is missing or undocumented.

This project includes a sky130-compatible standard cell generator written in Python using gdstk, four example cells (mux2i, maj3, dlrtp, dfrtp), and a TinyTapeout test chip that compares foundry cells against custom-generated ones. The test chip uses an instrumentation framework with a ring oscillator, clock divider, and shift registers to perform both direct and advanced tests at speed. Silicon tests confirmed basic functionality in direct output mode, but the author cautions against using the custom cells in serious designs due to limited testing.
